analysis.one_liner: Gives users of online platforms the right to see, control, and delete their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended, despite being introduced by a Democrat with Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require websites and apps that collect personal data to tell users up front that their data will be collected and shared, and to let them opt out. Users could get a free copy of their data, including a list of everyone it was sold or handed to, and companies would have to alert users within 72 hours if their data leaked. Enforcement would fall to the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of Americans who use social media, search engines, email, and mobile apps would gain real control over their personal data: advance notice of data collection, a choice to opt out, a free copy of their data with a list of who received it, deletion within 30 days of closing an account, and notification within 72 hours when their data is misused. State attorneys general would gain a new tool to sue violators on residents' behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Operators must tell users before they sign up that their personal data will be collected and used by the platform and third parties, and must offer an option to prohibit that collection, in terms of service written in clear, concise language [S2] [S3].
Users can get a free electronic copy of the personal data an operator has processed, including a list of each person who received that data, whether through sale or other means [S2] [S3].

Operators must notify users within 72 hours of learning that their personal data was transmitted in violation of the platform's privacy or security program, and offer options to erase the data and stop further dissemination [S2] [S3].

Personal data must become inaccessible no later than 30 days after a user closes their account, users must be able to withdraw consent as easily as they gave it, and operators must audit their privacy programs at least every two years [S3].

The bill closes two enforcement gaps: it lets the FTC police common carriers (currently exempt from FTC authority) and nonprofit organizations, and it lets state attorneys general bring civil actions in federal court over violations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms — social networks, ad networks, search engines, email services, mobile operating systems, and internet providers — would bear the cost of building disclosure and consent systems, honoring data access and deletion requests, running biennial audits, and facing FTC and state enforcement for violations. Telecom common carriers would lose their long-standing exemption from FTC jurisdiction for these practices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media, ad tech, and telecom firms

drawbacks.text: A user who opts out of data collection can be denied service or locked out entirely if their privacy election creates 'inoperability' in the platform — so the right to say no can come at the price of losing access to the service [S3].

Individuals get no right to sue on their own; enforcement runs only through the FTC and state attorneys general, and a state must pause its suit if the FTC brings its own action against the same defendant [S3].

The bill is built on notice and consent rather than restricting data collection itself: so long as a user clicks through, sweeping collection and third-party sharing remain lawful, which consumer groups criticized as inadequate in the broader 2019 federal privacy debate (general knowledge about the model's limits).

Compliance costs — audits, disclosure redesigns, and per-user data access and deletion systems — fall on every covered platform, a heavier lift for small companies than for the giants the bill targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy rights it creates — data access, deletion, breach notification, opt-out — are real and would apply to nearly every website and app Americans use. The honest caveats are significant: a user's opt-out is not absolute because platforms can cut off service, individuals cannot sue on their own, and the consent-based structure leaves the underlying data-collection economy intact. It would have raised the floor meaningfully, but not transformed it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2019, and the committee never took it up — no hearings, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 17, 2019, joined from the start by Sen. John Kennedy, making it bipartisan on day one [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
The bill gathered three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat — but no further action was ever recorded [S4].
The committee never reported the bill, and the complete action history ends with the referral; it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and the data-driven advertising business are better off, because no disclosure, access, or deletion requirements ever took effect and the collection-and-sale of user data continued under pre-existing rules. Telecom carriers also kept their FTC exemption.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor with Republican cosponsors (3 cosponsors: 2 R, 1 D) — and it stalled in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Online platforms and ad tech (social networks, ad networks, search, email, mobile operating systems)
industries.note: These companies profit from collecting and monetizing user data; the bill would have forced disclosure, honored opt-outs, free data access with a list of recipients, deletion on account closure, and 72-hour breach-style notification. Compliance costs and FTC/state enforcement exposure fall squarely on them.

Common carriers are currently exempt from FTC enforcement; the bill would have stripped that exemption for these privacy practices, exposing phone and internet providers to FTC action for the first time.
Nonprofits are subject to FTC enforcement only in narrow circumstances today; the bill would have made them directly enforceable-against for these privacy violations.
